level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: The page ranks depend on which page the surfer starts from. Right rule: For the random-surfer chain the long-run probabilities are the same for all starting pages (basic limit theorem); that is why RandomSurfer can start at page 0.

Applies LT (each step uses the row of the current state) unevenly: e.g. on some steps using the starting page's row instead of the current page's row. (here mixing in: "The page ranks depend on which page the surfer starts from")
Changing the start state keeps the limiting distribution (if the chain mixes); removing the random leap can break mixing; squaring the matrix gives two-step probabilities.
wrong rule: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks. Right rule: freq[i]/T is only an estimate: about 10^n moves for n-digit precision and many more for accuracy.

wrong rule: A result printed with many decimal places must be accurate to those places. Right rule: Printing %8.5f does not make the estimate accurate to 5 places; ensuring accuracy is often the hardest part.

Applies LT (increment after each move, divide by T after the loop) unevenly: e.g. incrementing the page before the move on some passes, or dividing inside the loop. (here mixing in: "A short simulation gives the exact page ranks")
Invariant: the counts sum to T, so the fractions sum to 1; dividing before casting ((double)(freq[i] / T)) or counting outside the loop breaks it.

wrong rule: a large integer literal is automatically long. Right rule: A sequence of digits is an int literal only if its value falls within the int range; for larger values the book advises the long type.
wrong rule: Java has no float literals. Right rule: A decimal literal ending in f is a float; without the f it is a double.
wrong rule: Java has no long literals. Right rule: An integer literal ending in L is a long.
wrong rule: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers. Right rule: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double.

Points to LT (each literal denotes one fixed value whose type is read from how it is written). Applied unevenly, a student reads 2.0 as an int in one place, or '7' as the number 7 in one expression and as a character in the next. (here mixing in: "a large integer literal is automatically long")
Rewriting a literal in another form keeps the value but changes the type, and so the operation: 10 / 3 is 3 but 10.0 / 3 is 3.333..., and "5" + 1 is "51" but 5 + 1 is 6.
wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (int t = 0; t < T; t++) makes exactly T moves; with <= it makes T + 1, while the ranks are still divided by T.

wrong rule: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks. Right rule: A simulation only estimates the ranks: about 10^n moves for n-digit precision, tens of thousands of moves for two accurate places and millions for three.

Applies LT (draw r, find next page, then freq[page]++) unevenly: e.g. counting the current page before the move on some passes, or resetting sum only on the first pass. (here mixing in: "< vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable")

wrong rule: A variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: r and sum are declared inside the t-loop body and are created anew on every move; freq and page must be declared before the loop to persist.

Changing the start page keeps the limit (mixing); increasing T keeps the estimates but makes them more accurate (about 10x moves per extra digit); changing < to <= or the division by T breaks the normalisation.

wrong rule: Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) == 2 is true. Right rule: A double is an approximation: Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) is 2.0000000000000004, so the == test is false; compare doubles with a tolerance.

wrong rule: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers. Right rule: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double, whatever its value: 207. is 207.0 and 2.3e4 is 23000.0, so int n = 2.3e4; does not compile.

Points to LT (at each operator the narrower operand is promoted, then the operation is done in double and rounded).
